scope: choosing tape archive or tape backup software for LTO drives and libraries: HSM and tiering to tape, S3 or file gateways to tape, media and video archives, research and HPC archives, compliance archives, leaving an old tape product, sizing a tape archive, for any size from one drive to petabytes
offTopicMsg: I only help you choose tape archive software. Describe your archive, for example: 300 TB of video, LTO-9 library, two sites, small team.
rules: A small site (under about 200 TB, one or two drives, one admin or a small budget) makes free_entry, common_skills and price_safety important (weight 4 or 5). Scale and tiering only matter when the visitor mentions petabytes, many drives or HSM.

Anything kept for ten years or longer (long term archive, research data, medical images, compliance records) makes formats and integrity important, and exit_ease too because the archive will outlive the product. Compliance, legal hold, WORM or audits make security and integrity important.

Video post production and broadcast need tapes other facilities can read, so formats (LTFS) matter, plus access and common_skills for small media teams; broadcasters with a MAM and an existing archive also need tiering and delivery. Offsite rotation or a vault makes media important; a cloud copy makes cloud important.
Petabytes, HPC, research computing or many drives make scale, tiering and hardware important. Vendor support required makes delivery important.

CERN Tape Archive is a physics scale open-source engine that needs the EOS or dCache stack, a catalogue database and scarce skills: exclude cta unless the visitor runs petabytes and has an in-house team that can run open-source storage without a vendor. Exclude it whenever the visitor needs vendor support.

Exclude a candidate only for a stated or clearly implied hard requirement taken from the facts, for example a required operating system the product does not run on (some run only on Windows or only on macOS), a need for vendor support, or a format the visitor will not accept. Never exclude a candidate only because it scores lower.

criteria.label: Drives and libraries
criteria.desc: support for current LTO generations up to LTO-10, enterprise tape drives and many library brands (Ledger: tape library and drive support)

criteria.label: Open tape formats
criteria.desc: writes LTFS or another open, documented format, so tapes stay readable without the product years later (Ledger: open formats and portability)

criteria.label: Data tiering
criteria.desc: policy based movement between disk, tape and cloud, HSM stubs, partial and fast recall (Ledger: data movement and tiering)

criteria.label: Integrity and fixity
criteria.desc: checksums, fixity checks, media verification, multiple copies and repack for long term preservation (Ledger: integrity and preservation)

criteria.label: Access: S3, NFS, SMB
criteria.desc: how users and applications reach the archive: S3 or Glacier style API, NFS, SMB, APIs (Ledger: access protocols)

criteria.label: Scale and throughput
criteria.desc: petabyte scale, many drives in parallel, high ingest and recall throughput (Ledger: scale and performance)

criteria.label: Security and WORM
criteria.desc: encryption and key management, WORM and retention lock, audit trails, access control (Ledger: security and compliance)

criteria.label: Media and vaulting
criteria.desc: tracking cartridges, offsite vaulting and rotation, media health, migration to new LTO generations (Ledger: media management and vaulting)

criteria.label: Cloud copy and hybrid
criteria.desc: a copy or tier in public cloud object storage next to tape (Ledger: cloud and hybrid)

criteria.label: Management and API
criteria.desc: admin interface, REST API, monitoring and automation (Ledger: management and automation)

criteria.label: Price and licence safety
criteria.desc: low buyer risk on price rises, licence rules, owner changes and the cost of staying supported (inverted Ledger commercial risk)

criteria.label: Easy to leave later
criteria.desc: little format, stack and skills coupling, so moving the archive away later is cheap (inverted Ledger technical lock-in)

criteria.label: Easy to start buying
criteria.desc: few purchase constraints: trial or free start, no bundled hardware or minimum purchase (inverted Ledger purchase constraints)

criteria.label: Common skills
criteria.desc: runs on skills and tools most storage admins already have, so a small team can run it (inverted Ledger skills and tooling coupling)

criteria.label: Vendor keeps promises
criteria.desc: release cadence, published roadmap and shipping what was announced (Ledger credibility)

guide: Sizing: native cartridge capacity is 6 TB for LTO-7, 12 TB for LTO-8, 18 TB for LTO-9 and 30 TB for LTO-10 (a 40 TB LTO-10 cartridge also exists). Use the visitor's LTO generation, or assume LTO-9 when they give none, and do not count compression. Cartridges = data now plus one year of growth, divided by native capacity, rounded up, times the number of copies. Assume two copies (one in the library, one offsite) unless the visitor says otherwise. Write the assumption in sizing, for example "LTO-9, 2 copies, 24 cartridges, 2 drives".

Drives: two or more for production so a drive can fail and reads can run beside writes; one drive is fine for a small archive under about 100 TB. Library slots: the onsite copy plus about 10 percent spare and a cleaning slot. Disk cache in front of tape: about one week of incoming data, or 5 to 10 percent of the archive for HSM.

Topology icons: the archive server or gateway (server icon, or nas for a small Windows or Mac archive box), the disk cache (storage icon), the tape library (library icon, put the drive count in the label such as "Library, 2 drives"), the offsite cartridge copy (tape icon in zone second, suggested when the visitor did not mention offsite), a cloud copy (object icon in zone cloud) only when the visitor mentions cloud or a third copy, where the data comes from (users, app or vm_host icon), and management (mgmt icon) for larger sites. Link labels: SAS, FC, S3, NFS or SMB, courier, replication.

Steps: 1 check that the product supports the visitor's drives and library, 2 pilot with a small data set and restore it, 3 set the policies (number of copies, retention, LTFS or the product's own format, encryption keys), 4 migrate the old archive or tapes when the visitor has one, 5 run a scheduled restore test and media health checks, then rotate the offsite copy.

Notices: the tape format from the facts (a proprietary format means the product is needed to read the tapes, LTFS means other tools can read them), the LTO read back rule (LTO-8 and LTO-9 drives read one generation back, LTO-10 drives read only LTO-10 cartridges, so plan a migration when changing generation), the licence model from the facts, keeping encryption keys safe, and storing cartridges cool and dry with labels and an offsite log.

faq.q: Which tape archive software is best for a small business?
faq.a: It depends on how much data you keep, your LTO drives, your operating system and who runs it. Type your setup into the advisor: it weights price, ease of leaving later and the features you need, then ranks 14 tape archive products with the Tape Archive Software Ledger scores.

faq.q: Why does the tape format matter so much?
faq.a: An archive often outlives the software that wrote it. Products that write LTFS or another open format leave tapes that other tools can read; a proprietary format means you need that product, or its vendor's tools, to get the data back. The advisor weighs this whenever you keep data for many years.

faq.q: Where do the scores come from, and is the advisor vendor neutral?
faq.a: From the Tape Archive Software Ledger 2026, which scores tape archive products on ten capability areas, vendor credibility, buyer risk and lock-in from public records only. TapeBackup.org is not paid by any vendor on the list, and the ranking is computed from those scores and the weights read from your message. The AI never writes a score.

line.en: Book a consulting call: we review your archive design, LTO sizing, tape format and migration plan.

candidates.name: IBM Storage Archive
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Scale-bound LTFS tiering. IBM keeps Storage Archive as the tape tier of Storage Scale and adds new IBM drives on the day they ship. The record shows LTO-8, LTO-9 and LTO-10 supported at launch and LTFS tapes that other tools can read, but no cloud tier, no file checksums and IBM libraries only. A buyer gets a portable tape format in exchange for a hard dependency on Storage Scale and IBM tape hardware. Formats: EE writes LTFS (SNIA 2.4) readable on any LTFS system; Space Management data sits in Storage Protect pools with no open-format statement; Export path: Exit path: read LTFS tapes with any LTFS implementation; namespace and stub mapping stay in Scale and EE metadata.

candidates.name: Quantum StorNext
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Media-era multi-tier HSM. Quantum keeps StorNext Storage Manager as a policy engine that moves files between disk, tape, object storage and public cloud tiers. The record shows broad library support, checksums and multi-copy repair since before 2016, but a release gap from 2023 to 2025 and LTO-10 arriving about 14 months after the drives. A buyer gets a mature multi-tier archive tied to the StorNext file system, from a vendor whose finances have been under strain since 2024. Formats: Default ANTF is Quantum-specific with no published spec; LTFS option stores files by object ID with the path in xattrs; Export path: LTFS and ANTF export/import with manifests into another.

candidates.name: HPE DMF
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: HPC HSM in maintenance. HPE runs DMF 7 as a database-backed HSM for large HPC file systems and has spent the last three releases on platform upkeep and a first public API. The record shows broad library support, per-block checksums and policy-driven tape generation moves, but a proprietary tape format, no encryption or WORM features, no LTO-10 and no release for 12 months. A buyer gets proven HPC scale on any major library in exchange for a format only DMF can read and an uncertain release pace. Formats: Proprietary DMF media format with zones and chunks; no documented reader outside DMF; Export path: Chunk-to-volume mapping lives in the Library Server and Cassandra.

candidates.name: Spectra BlackPearl
candidates.kind: S3 or file gateway to tape
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Appliance S3-to-tape gateway. Spectra is building BlackPearl into an S3 and Glacier-compatible object tier on its own tape libraries, with StorCycle feeding it from file storage. The record shows steady dated releases, LTO-10 support before the generation's launch and LTFS on tape with object names kept in extended attributes. The trade-off is hardware coupling: BlackPearl is a Spectra appliance, non-Spectra libraries need a paid key, WORM media is not supported and full release notes sit behind a support login. Formats: LTFS with object names in LTFS extended attributes; objects split into 64 GB blobs may span tapes, readability of split objects without BlackPearl not.

candidates.name: Versity ScoutAM
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Open-format HPC archive challenger. Versity is building ScoutAM into an exabyte archive for research sites that leave older HSMs, with an open S3 gateway and GPU data paths around it. The record shows open tar-based tapes, wide library support with LTO-10 within months, and large public deployments, but ScoutAM release notes are private and media management is barely documented. A buyer gets low format and contract lock-in from a small private vendor whose core product can only be checked through its own pages and customer stories. Formats: VSM tar variant readable with standard tar for files under about 64 GB, star above; ScoutAM claims open formats readable without.

candidates.name: Atempo Miria
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Broad data mover with tape archive. Atempo positions Miria as a data-movement engine that archives from NAS, HPC file systems and object stores to tape and cloud, and it kept shipping through receivership and a court-ordered sale. The public compatibility guides show wide library support, LTO-10 within about six months, TAR and LTFS on tape and KMS-based encryption, with four releases since early 2025. The trade-off is owner and lifecycle risk: new owners since 2025, a steady list of removed features and mandatory database moves, and no S3 or Glacier front end of its own. Formats: TAR (PAX) with metadata on tape and LTFS 2.5.1; WORM only with TAR; erasure-coded chunks need.

candidates.name: Grau XtreemStore
candidates.kind: S3 or file gateway to tape
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Quiet S3 Glacier tape store. Grau Data rebuilt XtreemStore around 2019 as an object store that puts S3 and S3 Glacier on tape, and it now sells it through partners and as a turnkey appliance with COMBACK. The public record shows a standard S3 Glacier interface, TAR containers in LTFS format that the vendor says are readable without its software, and new partner integrations in 2025 and 2026. The trade-off is thin evidence: no release notes, versions, compatibility list, encryption or checksum documentation, and prices only through resellers. Formats: TAR containers in LTFS format; how S3 keys and metadata map to TAR contents is not documented; Export path: Vendor says data.

candidates.name: QStar Archive Manager
candidates.kind: S3 or file gateway to tape
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Long-running multi-protocol tape gateway. QStar sells capacity-licensed software that puts SMB, NFS and S3 shares in front of almost any tape library, with Network Migrator for stub-based tiering and Global ArchiveSpace to spread one library over many nodes. Its dated compatibility lists show LTO-9 within about four months, LTO-10 listed before the specification and TS1170, but there are no public release notes and manuals come only on request. The trade-off for a buyer is a proprietary TDO format unless LTFS is chosen, thin public documentation, and nine unpatched CVEs from 2024 with no vendor response found. Formats: Choice per volume of proprietary TDO (no public.

candidates.name: PoINT Storage Manager
candidates.kind: S3 or file gateway to tape
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Small-vendor S3 Glacier on tape. PoINT pairs a Windows file tiering and HSM product with an S3 gateway that writes straight to tape and presents disk and tape as S3 Standard and Glacier classes. Its public revision tables show LTO-9 within three months, IBM LTO-10 at the specification date, TS1170, redundant drive paths and a free LTFS option added in 2026. The trade-off is a small private vendor with release notes behind a login, no published prices, and older PAG tapes in an erasure-coded PoINT format that needs PoINT's specification or tools to read. Formats: PSM writes LTFS (default) or MTF (WORM) with UDF-based archive volumes; PAG wrote only its own erasure-coded.

candidates.name: XenData
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Windows LTO archive appliance. XenData sells Windows-based LTO archive appliances and software, mostly to media companies, that present tape as a file system with S3 as a paid add-on and cloud tiers beside it. Its public release notes show LTO-8 and LTO-9 within about two months of launch, LTFS 2.4 and TAR on tape, partial-file restore and readers for several competitors' tape formats, with IBM LTO-10 added in 2026. The trade-off is a Windows-only stack with no REST management API, no software tape encryption or retention lock found, and some recent announcements (ALTO, X10) not yet visible in shipped releases. Formats: LTFS 2.4 on rewritable LTO-5 and later, or XenData.

candidates.name: Archiware P5
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Budget media archive with LTFS. Archiware sells P5 Archive as low-cost perpetual software that archives media projects to LTO, disk and cloud from almost any server, with LTFS pools, an S3 Glacier-class endpoint and policy-based data movement added since 2021. The public record is unusually complete: dated releases, a discontinuations page, list prices and NAB or IBC previews that shipped within a year, with LTO hardware encryption added in 2026. The trade-off is reach: no enterprise tape drives, no NFS or SMB view of the archive, no KMIP or WORM handling, and the native pool format can only be read by P5. Formats: Two pool formats: P5 native (proprietary, 'exclusively.

candidates.name: Telestream DIVA
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Broadcast object archive, many owners. Telestream is modernising DIVA into a Windows-based broadcast archive with cloud lifecycle tiers, faster tape migration and a web interface, and folding FlashNet customers into it. The public documents show wide library and enterprise-tape support, IBM LTO-10 about six months after launch, an open AXF format with LTFS since 2022 and a standalone reader since 2026, and four or more releases a year. The trade-off is owner and lifecycle risk: lenders took the company in 2025, the product has changed owner and name repeatedly, upgrades need new licences, and support windows are short. Formats: AXF (open, self-describing) and LTFS AXF.

candidates.name: YoYotta
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Mac LTFS archive for post-production. YoYotta is a small Mac application that archives camera and project media to LTFS tapes in standalone drives and libraries, now with up to four libraries and eight drives. The record shows LTO-8, LTO-9 and LTO-10 supported at launch, LTFS as the only write format with checksums carried on tape, and low public prices. The trade-off is scope: it runs only on macOS, has no encryption, WORM, policy tiering, network access or API, and since 2023 it needs a yearly licence to keep running jobs. Formats: Writes only LTFS 2.4, readable by any LTFS implementation; Export path: Tapes readable without YoYotta; checksums in extended attributes, MHL.

candidates.name: CERN Tape Archive
candidates.facts: Ledger archetype: Physics-scale tape engine. CERN is preparing CTA for LHC Run 4 with a PostgreSQL scheduler, gRPC administration and OpenTelemetry metrics, behind EOS or dCache disk buffers. The record shows an archive near one exabyte running at up to about 60 GB/s with tape verification, automated repack and public tags every few weeks, but no LTO-10 code yet, no file or S3 access of its own and a tape format that is not self-describing. A buyer gets free, proven large-scale tape software but must run the CERN stack around it without commercial support and must protect the catalogue, because file names do not live on tape. Formats: Own CTA/CASTOR AUL format, documented label by label.
